description: Official WhatsApp Business API pricing for 40+ countries. Compare Meta rates vs BSP markups.
fullText:
Compare Meta official rates vs average provider rates (15-25% markup)

Browse country-specific rate breakdowns and BSP comparisons for 20+ markets.

WhatsApp Business API cost depends on country and category. Example current Meta rates include US marketing USD 0.025; Brazil marketing USD 0.0625.

WhatsApp Business API is not completely free. Service conversations inside the 24-hour customer service window can be free, while marketing, utility, and authentication messages are paid according to Meta's country-specific rate card.

Meta groups WhatsApp Business messages into marketing, utility, authentication, and service categories. Marketing is used for promotions, utility for transactional updates, authentication for one-time passwords, and service for customer support conversations.

Many Business Solution Providers add a markup on top of Meta's official WhatsApp rates. This calculator shows the typical 15-25% BSP markup range so teams can compare the direct Meta rate with provider pricing.

WhatsApp Business pricing is based on billable business conversations and message categories, but teams often compare costs as an effective per message rate for planning and provider audits.

The rate comparisons are generated from the application's current Meta rate database and use Decimal arithmetic for currency amounts. When the database is updated, the homepage and country FAQ copy can reflect those current rates.

Some markets use local-currency billing. Brazil is represented in the current database with AUD rates, India is commonly billed in INR, and many other countries are shown in USD.

WhatsApp Business API pricing is built around conversation-based billing rather than a simple monthly subscription. A conversation is a 24-hour billing window opened when either the business or the customer sends the first qualifying message. During that window, the business can exchange messages with the same customer without opening a second charge in the same category. This is why the headline WhatsApp cost per message can be confusing: many pricing tables show a unit rate because it is easy to compare countries and categories, but the underlying billing event is the conversation window. The calculator above keeps the comparison practical by multiplying the current Meta rate by your planned volume, then showing how a typical provider markup changes the total. That makes WhatsApp API pricing easier to budget before you connect a CRM, support inbox, or marketing automation platform.

Country matters as much as category. Meta publishes different official rates for different destination markets, so a campaign sent to the United States will not necessarily cost the same as a campaign sent to Brazil, India, Indonesia, or Mexico. Currency also matters because many finance teams plan in USD even when the local market is billed in BRL, INR, or another currency. This page uses the rate data stored in the application database and converts totals through the same billing logic as the calculator, so the examples are tied to real pricing records instead of static copy. If your team is comparing WhatsApp Business pricing across vendors, always separate the official Meta component from the provider fee before deciding whether a quote is expensive.

Meta groups WhatsApp Business conversations into four categories: marketing, utility, authentication, and service. Marketing conversations are generally the most expensive because they include promotional campaigns, product launches, win-back offers, newsletters, and other business-initiated messages designed to drive revenue. Utility conversations cover operational updates such as order confirmations, appointment reminders, shipping alerts, account notices, and receipts. Authentication conversations are used for one-time passcodes, login verification, and security checks. Service conversations are customer-initiated support interactions, where the user contacts the business first and the business replies inside the customer service window.

The category determines the WhatsApp business message cost more than the template length or the number of words in the message. A short promotional coupon is still marketing, while a longer order-status update can still be utility if it is transactional and expected by the user. This classification matters because using the wrong template category can distort your forecast and may create compliance problems during template review. For planning, treat marketing as the budget-sensitive category, utility as the operational category, authentication as the security category, and service as the support category. Teams that understand these boundaries can forecast monthly spend more accurately and avoid comparing a marketing campaign quote against a utility notification rate.

Most businesses do not access the WhatsApp Business API directly. They work through a Business Solution Provider, often called a BSP, such as Twilio, MessageBird, 360dialog, WATI, or another regional provider. The BSP connects your application to WhatsApp, hosts messaging infrastructure, manages webhooks, provides dashboards, and often adds support tooling, template submission workflows, delivery reporting, and compliance guidance. In exchange, providers commonly add a 15-25% markup on top of Meta's official rates, sometimes bundled with platform fees, inbox seats, automation features, or minimum monthly commitments.

That markup is not automatically bad. If the provider reduces engineering time, improves deliverability visibility, or gives your support and marketing teams a usable interface, the extra cost may be cheaper than building and maintaining the integration yourself. The problem is opacity: many invoices blend the official Meta fee with the BSP fee, which makes it hard to know whether your WhatsApp Business API pricing is driven by message volume, destination country, category mix, or vendor margin. The most useful comparison is the one this calculator makes: official Meta total beside a provider-adjusted total. Once those numbers are separated, procurement can negotiate markup, engineering can evaluate direct integration, and growth teams can decide whether a campaign still has healthy unit economics.

Sending 1,000 marketing messages to US customers costs approximately $25.0000 at Meta's official rate, or $30.0000 with a typical BSP. That is a difference of $5.0000 per thousand marketing conversations before any separate platform subscription or seat fee is added. For a small campaign this gap may look modest, but at tens or hundreds of thousands of sends it becomes a real line item in the marketing budget.

For Brazil marketing traffic, the same 1,000-message planning scenario is $62.5000 at the official Meta rate and $75.0000 through a typical marked-up provider, leaving $12.5000 in avoidable markup for every thousand messages. Brazil is a good example of why country-level WhatsApp API pricing matters: a global average can hide the markets where campaigns are profitable and the markets where markup erodes contribution margin.

Utility notifications in India show a different cost profile. Sending 1,000 utility messages is approximately $1.4000 at Meta's official rate, compared with $1.6800 after a typical BSP markup. The markup difference is $0.2800 per thousand messages. Because utility traffic often scales with orders, bookings, deliveries, and account activity, even a low WhatsApp cost per message can become material when the business sends millions of operational notifications each month.

These examples are intentionally narrow: one country, one category, one volume, and one target currency at a time. Real invoices are usually a blend of marketing blasts, lifecycle utility messages, login verification, and customer support. To estimate a full month, model each traffic stream separately, apply the right destination country and category, then add the totals. That approach is more accurate than multiplying one blended rate across all messages, because the rate mix changes whenever your campaign calendar, customer geography, or support volume changes.

A common source of confusion is the difference between conversation billing and per-message planning. Meta bills around conversation windows, but businesses often forecast by message count because campaign tools, CRMs, and data warehouses track sends, deliveries, and replies as message events. When someone asks for the WhatsApp cost per message, they usually want a practical unit cost for budgeting rather than a statement about the exact billing primitive. This calculator uses per-message-style volume inputs so teams can compare Meta rates and provider rates quickly, while still explaining that the billed unit is tied to the conversation category and 24-hour window.

The distinction matters most when a customer sends multiple replies or when a business sends several follow-up messages inside the same open conversation. Those extra interactions may not create a new charge if they stay within the active window and category rules. On the other hand, starting a new business-initiated conversation after the window closes can create a new billable event. For forecasting, use message volume as a simple first-pass model, then refine it with your actual conversation open rates, reply rates, and support patterns once you have production data.

WhatsApp also includes free or lower-cost situations that can change the final invoice. When a customer messages your business first, you can respond inside the customer service window without treating every reply like a new outbound marketing push. Entry points from Facebook or Instagram ads can also create free messaging windows for eligible ad-to-WhatsApp conversations. These rules are valuable for support and acquisition teams because they reward conversations that begin with user intent. They do not eliminate the need to understand WhatsApp Business API pricing, but they do mean that two companies with the same total message count can pay different amounts depending on who initiated the conversation and how quickly the business replied.

The fastest way to reduce cost is to make your category mix honest and intentional. Do not send promotional content as utility, but do avoid classifying operational messages as marketing just because the template was written by a growth team. Next, negotiate BSP markup once you know your official Meta baseline; a provider is easier to evaluate when you can show the exact difference between official rates and marked-up rates. Third, batch and target marketing campaigns carefully. Sending fewer, better-segmented promotions often improves return on spend more than chasing the cheapest provider. Fourth, monitor country-level rate changes because a campaign that works in one market may not work in another. Finally, review invoices for platform fees, minimums, failed-message policies, and currency conversion spreads, since the visible WhatsApp business message cost is only one part of the total vendor bill.

For teams that send at scale, the right operating rhythm is monthly. Export your actual sends by country and category, compare the official Meta component with the provider component, and update your forecast before the next campaign calendar is approved. If the provider markup is small and the tooling saves time, keep it. If the markup grows faster than the value of the tooling, consider renegotiating, switching BSPs, or moving some traffic closer to Meta's official API. The goal is not always to pay the absolute lowest rate; it is to know exactly what you are paying for and whether that cost supports the customer experience and revenue outcome you expect.

fullText:
Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children

Veteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.

The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:

Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance

At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.

In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk once

Gibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X.com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.

Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear of civilisational breakdown

Musk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.

To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in action

Recently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.

Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-elected

In the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.

The godfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next election

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”

fullText:
The whole payments backend module, which I specifically told him to work together with me (I do frontend), was vibe-coded by him in one single day.

How nice, to not have to discuss with the human being who will be using your code and knows what he wants, and instead work with a sycophantic "yes man" AI right?

All 5,236 additions to the Github PR, including a documentation that is so blatant of AI redundancies (for example, saying that an error returns "400" on the API).

I understand that AI doesn't know that I know what a 400 is, but my friend should at least read that document and know better.

So here's the sad part. I understand y'all vibe-coding features and being 10x engineer and way faster than me.

But I just went to test the PR...

He didn't even TRY the endpoints.

It takes two minutes to run the endpoints that Don Claudio so happily added to Bruno.

He clearly didn't read the documentation as there was a lot of stuff missing. Stupid explanations about a "returns 400 on error" but missing info on where to get API keys.

And I specifically told him, when we started this project, that he should be very careful of falling into the AI trap of letting his cognitive abilities decline.

"Yes, yes, no worries man I know what I'm doing".

Well, as much as people lose all their muscle by been bed-ridden, he's lost all his brain by being AI Assisted™️.

THIS is what I am so against when people use AI for everything.

And I know, some of you will say "but that ain't me, haha, I can sit in my couch and watch TV all day and not exercise and keep all my muscle!"

Well wait until you go play a basketball game with your pals and you'll realize you're out of breath in two minutes.

I know it's a losing battle for the few of us who learned to program and still program mostly by hand because we love the amount of stimulation it brings our brains.

My friend used to be one of those people. But I think there's almost nobody left.

Those days are gone, and I'm still grieving, but I think this is my very last battle.

After this project, I'm done. I might turn into a yoga teacher.

title: Why cleaning up after Burning Man is 'awesome business'
description: Burning Man is all about "Leave No Trace." But what happens to the tons of trash once it leaves the playa?
fullText:
NIXON, NV — Sitting on a dusty lawn chair alongside the road, Marc Lowery is turning Burning Man's trash into his own personal treasure at $10 a bag.

Burning Man is the world's largest "Leave No Trace" event, but that applies only to physical trash on the dry lakebed where this year 62,000 attendees partied for a week. Just as Burners are required to bring in all the food and water they need for the week, they're also required to remove all their trash, down to every last bit of glitter.

In a roadside pullout surrounded by more than a dozen dumpsters and roll-off trash containers, Lowery watches as his family and a team of college students swarm the dusty vehicles as they pull off to hand over their trash.

Lowery, 45, charges $5 for a small trash bag and $10 for big ones. He also collects used gas cans, dusty chairs, battered bikes and gallons upon gallons of water.

International Burning Man attendees, he said, have to buy almost everything they need once they arrive in the United States, and then leave behind whatever won't fit in their suitcases.

"Whatever they can't take with them, they dump out," Lowery said. "It's pretty crazy watching."

Lowery donates the leftover water and gas to fellow members of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation, and sells some of the other things people drop off.

"It's a cycle," he said. "People come out here and spend what they need, and then give us whatever they don't want."

Burning Man's leave-no-trace ethic is deeply woven into the annual event's fabric. Camps are responsible for policing the sand where they set up, and Burning Man officials name-and-shame campers who fail to thoroughly clean up in an annual report.

The event's federal permit is predicated on removing all physical traces of what attendees call "MOOP" — matter out of place.

"There is no event on the planet this size with no trash cans," said Burning Man CEO Marian Goodell.

Nevertheless, the organization's critics note that while Black Rock City's temporary residents leave nothing behind on the dry lake bed, the event still has a significant environmental impact.

There's the fuel they burn to drive or fly there, the diesel generators powering many camps and their massive sound stages, even the air pollution caused by burning the wooden Man and Temple each year.

Last year, 85% of attendees arrived in a vehicle, and 32% came from California. Nearly 20% of Burners came from a country other than the United States or Canada, often flying from Europe or Asia, according to the official Black Rock City Census.

Goodell said the Burning Man nonprofit, which stages the event, is committed to reducing its environmental footprint, in large part by slashing the amount of diesel burned to make electricity. And an increasing amount of the propane that powers the flame-throwing dragons and other art cars comes from renewable sources.

Further, both the organization and attendees are increasingly using solar panels and batteries, rather than small generators, to power everything from air conditioning to art cars.

Burning Man has committed to being carbon negative by 2030. With the help of donors, Burning Man has invested heavily in everything from large-scale solar installations to composting toilets that don't need to be emptied. This year's city also offered free solar charging for electric vehicles and e-bikes.

Another program on the playa collects food scraps that then get composted and used to grow food at Burning Man's Fly Ranch, according to the organization's sustainability report.

Burning Man officials note that while their event receives significant criticism, the same people who attend would likely otherwise be on a different vacation, consuming a similar amount of resources.

Still, Goodell said she's heard the environmental criticisms, and believes the event can do more to shape behavior far from the playa. Among past high-profile attendees are Elon Musk and Ben & Jerry's cofounder Ben Cohen, and Burning Man officials always encourage participants to take the lessons learned on the playa back to the "default world" they live in.

"Burners are always trying to make things better," Goodell said. "Whatever humanity does, we're doing it here."

At Burning Man, the sole exception to the "no garbage left behind" system exists for attendees who arrived on the "Burner Express" bus shuttles. Launched more than a decade ago to help reduce the number of vehicles driving from Reno, Nevada, and San Francisco to the Black Rock Desert and back, the service provides each rider with a single trash bag and another for recycling.

Calling Burning Man: Free pay phone connects strangers worldwide

Burning Man's approach to trash and sustainability helped attract first-time Burner Hanz Atia, 32, of Cambridge, Massachusetts. As she and her husband dropped off their trash and recycling, Atia said she thought hard about all the one-time-use items a week of camping often requires, from plastic water bottles to disposable coolers.

"As we were preparing, I tried to be very conscious about buying things we wouldn't just use once," said Atia, who works in sustainability issues. "Trash doesn't ever just disappear."

Off the playa, Lowery and his crew were doing their best to remove the trash, even if it doesn't actually disappear. He said he takes a week off each year to run the trash collection point, one of several along the narrow road running south to Interstate 80.

Trash dots that road, from bags that apparently fell off vehicles to shiny reflective window shades, mangled bikes and other detritus.

Lowery said he finds it amusing to see how much stuff Burners leave behind. But he's not terribly upset about it, at $10 a bag.

"There's always going to be trash. You just have to put it in the right place and do the right thing," he said. "It's an awesome business."

This article originally appeared on Reno Gazette Journal: Why cleaning up after Burning Man is 'awesome business'

title: I took a 6-figure job at Amazon after stepping away from full-time entrepreneurship. A chance meeting led me back to my business.
description: Seun Phillips returned to his business, Stemnetics, after a one-year stint at Amazon. He used his tech experience to expand STEM education programs.
fullText:
Seun Phillips took a six-figure job at Amazon after stepping back from entrepreneurship.

A chance meeting with a principal prompted Phillips to return to his business, Stemnetics, full time.

He says Amazon's customer obsession and frugality still guide his work.

This as-told-to essay is based on an interview with Seun Phillips, the 42-year-old founder of Stemnetics, who is based in Los Angeles. It has been edited for length and clarity.

I was always interested in technology. My family got our first computer when I was in the third grade, and my four brothers and I would always game together. I was good at math and science, and my father said I should think about becoming an engineer.

In 2006, I graduated from the University of Michigan with a degree in electrical engineering. We had a career fair on campus. I remember my next class was about to start, but I saw Motorola. I decided to drop just one more résumé. They called me, and I got through the interview process. I became an electrical engineer focused on accessory compatibility for Motorola in Illinois.

I went on to become an entrepreneur, with a stint at Amazon in between, where I learned lessons I still use in my business today.

I launched Project Syncere in Chicago in March 2009. Its mission is to create pathways for underrepresented students to pursue careers in STEM. This was my first experience running a business, apart from selling CDs in high school. I'm still on the board.

I met my wife and moved to Detroit to be with her. We weren't looking to expand Project Syncere to another state, so in January 2014, I launched Stemnetics in Michigan, which runs hands-on STEM programs for kids.

I got a job as the vice president of education and engagement at the Michigan Science Center. I took the job because I had my first child and needed more financial stability.

I hired a full-time teacher and a part-time teacher through Indeed and Craigslist, so they kept the program running while I used my science center earnings to bootstrap the company. I wanted to keep Stemnetics running because I saw the potential.

I started searching for new roles, and a former colleague told me he was hiring at Amazon Robotics. The role involved identifying companies and startups developing technologies that could improve fulfillment, logistics, and supply chain operations. I understood the startup ecosystem, and I like bringing people together. I was interested.

I had six back-to-back interviews over Zoom, each centered on a different Amazon leadership principle. The ones that stayed with me were customer obsession, frugality, ownership, and bias for action. I still use them at Stemnetics: stay focused on who you serve, move quickly, and find a resourceful way forward without compromising quality.

I remember starting the interview process at 6 a.m. because I'm on Pacific Time. The last interview was with the person who ended up being my manager. I was hired with a six-figure salary.

My role focused on building partnerships with companies and startups.

I worked remotely, but I visited the office and a fulfillment center many times. The Amazon environment was very different from other Big Tech offices I heard about: There were standard cubicles and labs where you could see the technology being tested.

I wanted to see the robots in action at a fulfillment center so I could understand how everything moved. I'm very big on the why. I'm seeking partnerships, but why is it important? It was nice to see.

One thing I found really useful at Amazon was working backward. You start by writing a future press release describing the customer benefit you hope to create. It gives you a North Star for what you're building.

Another cool concept at Amazon was a Wellness Day. You're not supposed to use that as a vacation day — you're supposed to use it for professional development, catching up, anything that would support your mental health. My manager's manager made sure no meetings were scheduled, so it was truly all about wellness.

After about a year at Amazon, I was watching football at a sports bar when I started talking to a school principal. He told me he was trying to build a STEM lab. I told him I ran STEM programs, and we decided to meet.

I demonstrated the program at his school. Then the district heard about it. That was the moment I realized Stemnetics was ready for my full attention.

I was very close with my manager at Amazon, and there were opportunities there, but I think it was more about me betting on myself.

I used some of the Michigan curriculum to expand in California, and I'd pack the containers with teaching materials I'd bought on Amazon until the wee hours of the morning. My wife would come down, and our whole living room would be full of teaching materials, and then I'd drop the boxes off at different schools. I'd also teach the students and train the other instructors.

Today, we have an office with storage facilities for teaching materials and program managers who help with the training process. I've surpassed my Amazon earnings, we have over 35 employees, and we have over 30 programs running in Michigan and California. The impact we're making is very gratifying.

My favorite part of my job is visiting the classroom and seeing students screaming with excitement. We're really focused on sparking kids' interest and finding ways to help them become great problem solvers, think critically, be resilient, and be confident.

title: Designers should not fear being replaced by AI, industry leaders say
description:
Firms are more likely to use technology as ‘the intern in the office’ than as a replacement for skilled staff
Professional designers should not feel “threatened” by the rapid growth of generative AI, according to business leaders, despite fears over job losses in the sector.
With design and film production companies and manufacturers all adopting AI at an accelerating pace, industry bodies said the technology would be used to enhance the work of designers rather than replace them.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Firms are more likely to use technology as ‘the intern in the office’ than as a replacement for skilled staff

Professional designers should not feel “threatened” by the rapid growth of generative AI, according to business leaders, despite fears over job losses in the sector.

With design and film production companies and manufacturers all adopting AI at an accelerating pace, industry bodies said the technology would be used to enhance the work of designers rather than replace them.

Mat Hunter, the chief executive of the Design Council – a charity which champions the industry – said that while AI was increasingly being used by designers, “they are using it to add value”.

He said: “We are aware that technology always displaces people with new ways of working. However, we believe in the imagination and inventiveness of designers to find opportunities. We believe the UK needs more professional designers, so overall employment should continue to grow.”

Deborah Dawton, chief executive of the Design Business Association, said: “What protects great designers from AI is skill, experience, empathy and deep understanding of the sectors they operate in. So, no, [workers] shouldn’t feel threatened if they operate at this level.”

Earlier this year research, conducted by The King’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence and the Policy Institute, showed 57% of the public think AI will lead to widespread unemployment. Last week, freelancers including designers told the Guardian they were picking up “soulless” work correcting AI errors.

The Design Council said on Monday that its analysis showed the sector – which covers everything from the design of household products and fashion to building and transport design – had grown by 40% between 2019 and the end of 2023, beating the economy’s 23% average rate of expansion and leapfrogging the size of the retail industry.

Research funded by the council for its triennial overview – Design Economy 2026 – showed that sectors like construction, services and manufacturing support 2.27m design jobs, and that there has been a 15% increase in employment between 2020 and 2025.

While the figures estimating the size of the industry pre-date the arrival of dominant AI tools including ChatGPT and Claude, the employment figures to the end of last year indicate that their use has done little so far to affect the demand for workers with design skills.

Hunter said design was often considered to be an add-on or nice-to-have, but was essential to industries from advanced manufacturing to digital services.

“People don’t realise design is everywhere and is about trying to make things usable,” he said.

He added that the government’s consolidation of hundreds of public sector websites into one consistent design was an example of improvements in a service that can be supported by designers.

Dawton said AI was being used as a substitute for the work done by human designers, but “rip-offs have been happening for a very long time – AI hasn’t enabled that”.

The industry went through a similar transition when companies began using computer-aided design software, displacing draughtspeople, but Dawton said modern workers could find jobs elsewhere in the industry as it expands.

She added: “The key thing to remember is that these copycats look the same but they aren’t the same. The materials, finishes, methods of manufacture, assembly, colour, etc, mean that they are very different products.”

Over the longer term, she said: “We have to adapt to any technological change that takes place around us. The difference with the design industry is that large chunks of it drive that change.

“For most in business, efficiency/optimisation is the main conversation around AI. Designers have a second conversation with AI, which is about the potential it opens up in the hands of a creator.”

Andrew Duff, head of the Society of Garden and Landscape Designers, said many people working in his industry were nervous about AI. He said design companies were more likely to use AI as “the intern in the office” than as a replacement for skilled staff.

The Design Council report said some regions had grown strongly over the last eight years, though from a low base. There was an 88% increase in income from design across all industries in Wales and a 67% rise in the north-east of England. The south-east remained the hub for design industries, accounting for £43.3bn of gross value added (GVA) – a calculation of income from economic activity – compared with just £3.1bn in the north-east from a UK total of £136.7bn.

Its contribution was larger than the UK’s retail sector, worth £114bn, and nearly twice the size of the accommodation and food service industry, worth £70bn.

Hunter said a lack of skilled workers was a bigger problem than AI after entries for design and technology GCSEs declined by 68% over the decade to 2024.

Dawton said: “We need specialist teachers and equipment in schools if we’re going to inspire the next generation of world shapers at an early age.”

fullText:
If you’ve been into side projects, you’ve probably seen countless times the story of someone building something really big and complex, launching it, and having 0 users. With the AI era we’re living in, this will become even more common since software is cheaper to make.

I’ve worked on many side projects over the years, some with big ambitions and some very small, to solve a specific personal challenge. And that’s fine, I love to work on something that allows me to be fully creative without restrictions, but if your goal is to create a business, the starting place needs to be a bit different.

Instead of working for months and launching something, thinking you can be really big and have thousands of random people all over the world using your product, start with one person. The auto repair shop owner down the street, a lawyer you know, the restaurant manager, a teacher at your kids’ school. Start with that particular person and their specific challenges, and think of ways you can address them.

Perhaps they don’t need your service or SaaS software for that, but if it makes their lives easier in any way (saving time or money, or making them feel better), you have a business opportunity.

Build something with that person in mind, watch very closely how they operate, and start using your first version, and then, once a couple of months have passed, start expanding. Ask colleagues, talk to other people in that sector, and see who else might be interested.

If you’ve been able to help one person, you can help two, and three.

Things take time, of course, but if this is a side project, you have time on your side; there’s no VC asking for growth charts.

A small piece of strategic advice: start with the marketing side as soon as possible. Landing page, social content, SEO… They take time to show up on Google and other places, so the sooner you start, the better.

At some point, people will start looking for your solution and finding you, rather than the other way around. At that point, congratulations! You have a business.

A move for Monaco striker Folarin Balogun collapsed after the 25-year-old changed his mind following a medical at the club's Finch Farm training base.

The United States international emerged as a late target after Guinea-Bissau striker Beto completed a permanent switch to Serie A club Fiorentina.

The Toffees also explored deals for Manchester United forward Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa frontman Tammy Abraham but were unable to convince either to join.

They did sign Jack Grealish on a season-long loan deal from Manchester City, but lost star attacker Iliman Ndiaye to City in a deal worth £65m.

"I am disappointed that we didn't do more business and things didn't go our way in the end," Moyes said.

"Sometimes in football you have to live with disappointments and move on, and we will."

Issues with Balogun's medical meant Everton and Monaco renegotiated the initial £40m agreement.

Both clubs signed a deal sheet before the transfer window closed at 23:00 BST to provide extra time to complete the transfer only for Balogun to have a change of heart and walk away.

"It wasn't anyone's fault and ultimately it happens in football as the player had a problem in his medical and that was simply it," Moyes added.

"There are no other stories behind it. That is exactly what happened."

Moyes said that part of selling Ndiaye, who scored 15 goals and delivered four assists in 67 Premier League games for the Toffees, was to help provide funds for signings.

They failed to secure defender Kenny Tete after Fulham could not find a suitable replacement, but right-back Ainsley Maitland-Niles did arrive from Lyon for £3m.

"We were looking to get some money in," Moyes said.

"We lost Iliman Ndiaye, which is someone who we definitely didn't want to lose, but sometimes it is difficult when the likes of Man City come along.

"Some things went against us and some things we could have done better. Ultimately we didn't want to lose a lot of the different players but for reasons that had to happen."

fullText:
As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands

Pokémon’s success over the last 30 years has seen it grow from a much-loved Game Boy classic, to a world-dominating brand with TV shows, spin-off games, toys and even a theme park. The trading card game is a huge part of that, with more than 85bn cards printed over its lifetime, and the appetite for them shows no signs of slowing down. Packs get snapped up after release so quickly it’s now almost impossible to find them in shops, and a booming resale market is driving the hobby into murky waters.

One card recently sold for an eye-watering £12m, and an increasing number of people have gotten into the collecting business on the hunt for huge profits, leading to a rise in thefts targeting card shops. More recently though, some small businesses have reported that their sales have been hit by thieves targeting envelopes within Royal Mail, leading to thousands in lost revenue.

Ben Thyer, owner of Bath TCG – a card specialist store in the Bath area, is one of those affected. “We always get the odd parcel going missing, but because it was sporadic, we put that down to unfortunate incidents,” Thyer tells the Guardian. “Then [in late July], we had a message [from a customer] with pictures of a cut-open envelope, and the cards were missing. Then there was a second, and then a third, and then there were seven – all of them from the same batch shipped on the same day. We asked for images from each person, and every envelope had been Sellotaped … we don’t use Sellotape because we have brand new envelopes, and we use our own labels over the seals. It’s clear someone had done it deliberately.”

The images, seen by the Guardian, show that the mailed envelopes were tampered with in the exact same way. Thyer considers it clear that this was a targeted theft rather than a coincidence. Fortunately, those particular cards weren’t of high value, but he has since had to close down online card sales, considering the risk of theft and damaged reputation to his business to be too high. By stopping those sales he has now lost out on £4,000-6,000 of potential revenue, a huge amount for a small business.

Bath TCG is not the only card sales business to be affected, and the issue is not just affecting Pokémon cards. Daniel Stack, director of Mana Rock Games – a specialist in selling Magic: The Gathering cards – has also had issues with Royal Mail items going missing. His business is also based in Bath and was affected over similar dates to Bath TCG’s.

“I realised it was theft when two customers in different parts of the country sent me pictures of their packages already open with the contents missing, within minutes of each other,” Stack said. “We’d previously had one sent to France turn up the same way a couple of weeks before, but I put it down to the buyer taking a bit of a chance that I’d have no way to hold them to account for pretending there had been an issue. In total we’ve had about £120-worth stolen so far – we had previously sent over 1,200 orders without any issues.”

Stack also halted online sales for a week, costing him £500 in revenue. Other sellers in the area have mentioned similar problems to him. Unfortunately, as most card businesses in the UK use CardMarket to sell online, it’s the buyer who picks the delivery method, and most often they use Royal Mail services. Cards are often sent in distinctive hard-backed envelopes to protect the contents, often with shop branding on stickers or seals.

Royal Mail is investigating the issue and liaising with the affected businesses. A spokesperson told the Guardian: “The safety and security of mail is a top priority and we take any reports of theft very seriously. We investigate concerns thoroughly and take action where necessary, including working with law enforcement.” Investigations are still ongoing; in the meantime, businesses must choose between risking theft and damaged reputation for their stores, or halting online sales and losing revenue.

With a new, highly sought-after 30th anniversary Pokémon card set due to release this month, retailers are already anticipating an increase in scalper and reselling activity, leading to even more potential for thieves to target those selling cards online. We asked the Pokémon Company for comment on how they’re dealing with increased demand and the rise in thefts, but they have yet to respond.

title: FACT FOCUS: Trump claims US banks cannot operate in Canada. That's not true
description: Asked about the trade war with Canada on Wednesday, President Donald Trump falsely claimed that U.S. banks are not allowed to do business with its neighbor to the north.  The allegation came during a ...
fullText:
Asked about the trade war with Canada on Wednesday, President Donald Trump falsely claimed that U.S. banks are not allowed to do business with its neighbor to the north.

The allegation came during a meeting with U.S. travel executives in the Oval Office, after a reporter asked Trump whether there are plans for renewed trade talks between the two countries.

Experts say that although they may face restrictions, U.S. banks are not forbidden from operating in Canada.

Here's a closer look at the facts.

TRUMP: "They have their banks here, Bank of Canada, all of their big banks — big, beautiful banks. I think they have six or seven major banks here. We don't have our banks there. You know why? They don't allow it."

THE FACTS: There are currently 15 U.S.-based banks operating out of Canada, either as branches or subsidiaries, according to a spokesperson for the Canadian Bankers Association. Certain restrictions can make it difficult for U.S. banks to compete north of the border, experts say, but they are free to enter the market. There are eight Canadian banks operating in the U.S., according to the Federal Reserve's most recent data. The Bank of Canada is not one of them — it is Canada's central bank, equivalent to the Federal Reserve in the U.S., not a commercial enterprise.

"I think some confusion arises from the differences between the U.S. and Canadian regulatory systems," said James Thompson, a professor of finance at the University of Waterloo in Canada's Ontario province. "U.S. banks are certainly permitted to operate in Canada, but how they choose to enter the Canadian market affects what they can do."

There are three categories of banks in Canada — Schedule I, Schedule II and Schedule III. Canadian-owned banks are Schedule I. There are six major Schedule I banks whose combined assets eclipse those of the 28 smaller banks in the country.

Foreign entities can choose to operate as either Schedule II or Schedule III banks. Schedule II banks are foreign-owned subsidiaries incorporated in Canada that fall under essentially the same banking framework as banks owned domestically. Schedule III banks are branches of foreign banks that are not incorporated in Canada and therefore face regulatory restrictions such as high deposit minimums. Most U.S.-owned banks operate in Canada as Schedule III institutions.

Nathalie Bergeron, a spokesperson for the Canadian Bankers Association, said that U.S.-based bank branches and subsidiaries operating in Canada have combined assets of approximately $124.6 billion in Canadian dollars (US$904 million) — more than half of all assets held by foreign bank subsidiaries and branches.

"These banks specialize in a range of financial services, including corporate and commercial lending, treasury services, credit card products, investment banking and mortgage financing," she said. "They serve not only customers with cross-border business activities, but also Canada's domestic retail market."

Among the U.S. banks doing business in Canada are J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, Citibank, Bank of America, Capital One, and Wells Fargo.

Both Schedule II and Schedule III banks face restrictions due to Canadian banking regulations. Jeremy Kronick, a financial and monetary policy expert who is president and CEO of the Canadian C.D. Howe Institute think tank, explained that Schedule III banks cannot accept deposits below $150,000 (US$72,529). This means most people won't be able to use them as their retail bank. He added that since Schedule II banks are separate legal entities from their foreign parent company, they need their own local capital and liquidity structures — an inefficient option from the bank's perspective.

Such restrictions may be the reason the majority of U.S.-owned banks choose not to do business over the border. There are more than 3,700 domestically-owned commercial banks in the U.S., according to the Federal Reserve, compared to the 15 with a presence in Canada.

"Canada is a relatively small market, and incumbent Canadian banks are already very large institutions with established brands, extensive branch networks and longstanding customer relationships," said Thompson. "For a U.S. bank contemplating entry, building the infrastructure necessary to compete for Canadian retail customers would be expensive, while initially capturing only a small share of an already relatively small market."

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Iraola happy with signings as Barcola set for debut
description: Manager Andoni Iraola discusses Liverpool's transfer business, the arrival of Bradley Barcola and keeping Cody Gakpo.
fullText:
Andoni Iraola says he is "very happy" with all of Liverpool's signings since his arrival and that it is down to him to "develop" the squad.

Liverpool had four major incomings this summer, including the £123m purchase of Bradley Barcola from Paris St-Germain.

Barcola will be available for selection for Liverpool's Premier League game against Ipswich Town on Friday.

The Reds opted against strengthening at right-back and in central midfield and Iraola has defended that decision.

"Do I want more signings? In the end, the club has decided those signings we have done are the ones that will improve our team, improve the positions," Iraola said.

"There were other options that we decided not to take for different reasons, sometimes sporting or economical. It didn't make sense in the market for those moves.

"But I'm happy now. I have a lot of quality in the team. Now it is the moment is for me and the players to develop what we have."

A £60m deal for centre-back Jeremy Jacquet, who arrived this summer, was done in January and, under Iraola, Liverpool have signed winger Victor Munoz from Osasuna for £34.5m and defender Ronald Araujo on loan from Barcelona.

Liverpool elected not to replace Curtis Jones, who joined Inter Milan in a £30m deal.

Jones made 49 appearances for Liverpool last season, and Iraola now has four senior central midfielders to chose from in Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch, Alexis Mac Allister and Wataru Endo, as well as youngster Trey Nyoni.

"In midfield we have good numbers," said Iraola.

"Now it's a matter of getting the right calls from myself. I'm finding now the best combinations and we are going through a period now where we will play a lot of games and we'll have a chance to see the options we have and the combinations we have.

Iraola said he was "glad to keep Cody Gakpo because he is a valuable player" after Manchester City had a £80m bid for the Dutchman rejected.

Gakpo has one goal and one assist in Liverpool's first two league games of the season - both of which ended in draws.

Iraola is yet to win a game as Liverpool boss but there certainly wasn't any sense of panic when he spoke to the media for the first time since the transfer window ended.

Iraola said he feels "much more comfortable" now that he knows what players he has to work with and insisted that the responsibility is on him to "develop" what Liverpool have and that it is about "coaching and taking decisions".

Liverpool admired Iraola's trait of developing players across his coaching career when they came to appointing him, and now is the time to see what he can do.

Admittedly, Liverpool have lacked quality depth in their first two games, albeit with a number of players out injured, and Iraola's insistence that he is "very happy" with all the signings they made suggests that there is a general feeling of satisfaction internally with the summer activity.

When you include the Jacquet signing, Liverpool had the highest net-spend of any Premier League side this summer.

"I want to win. I need to win," said Iraola, after his side drew 2-2 against Newcastle and Nottingham Forest.

It is early doors still, but Iraola knows three points at Ipswich will make things a lot more comfortable for him.

title: CEO and President of Good Good no longer with company after weekslong ad scandal
description: It appears that the Good Good Golf saga is circling towards a conclusion. fullText:
It appears that the Good Good Golf saga is circling towards a conclusion.

On Wednesday, a report from Lucia Moses at Business Insider revealed an internal memo that was shared to Good Good employees which noted that co-founder and CEO Matt Kendrick "decided to step down," and relatively new Good Good president Joe Flannery "has chosen to part ways as well."

For those who have been blessedly, relatively unaware of this story until now, a quick recap. Good Good Golf is a YouTube channel turned all-around golf brand that was one of the biggest success stories in the sport's social media space. Good Good had partnerships across golf brands, sold plenty of merch, and had even was set to sponsor a PGA Tour this fall.

Two weeks ago, an ad produced by Good Good for a new driver cobranded with Callaway was released over Callaway's social channels. That ad depicted Garrett Clark, one of the founders of Good Good, tackling a woman who dared to touch his driver. The reaction to the ad was immediate and obvious, as none of the brands working alongside Good Good wanted to be associated with violence against women in defense of a golf club. Callaway quickly pulled the ad.

An initial apology missed the mark, and crucially, did not break down just where in the chain of command things fell apart to allow such a bad idea to go public. From there, more apologies followed. Clark posted an eight-minute long front-facing video apology to social media explaining that the ad was meant to be a parody of the film Obsession.

"Once I watched it back and it got posted, my skin was crawling. I was cringing," Clark said in the video. "I thought it was the worst ad known to man."

It wasn't enough to stem the bleeding of partners and sponsorships, as many of the brands tied to Good Good decided it was better to part ways than stick with the brand through the struggle. Those departures were followed by a late-night social media post from Kendrick, in which he said that Callaway had approved the ad and then dropped them in "a coordinated media blitz."

Since then, people have been fired at both Callaway and Good Good in relation to the ad's release, but the departures of Kendrick and Flannery are the clearest signs yet that Good Good is looking to truly move past the situation and turn the page.

As Matt Yoder wrote for us earlier this week, the downfall of Good Good is a case study in how not to handle a crisis that will be studied for quite some time.
